summary: Defines mechanisms for SIP user agents behind firewalls and NATs to keep client-initiated connections open so proxies can deliver requests to them. It helps handle networks where the server cannot open a connection to the client.

plainLanguage.summary: If you are behind a locked gate, no one can knock. So you open a line to them and keep it open, and they talk through it.

questions: how do sip phones work behind nat
what is a sip flow token
subtitle: How SIP phones behind NATs and firewalls keep connections to their servers open so calls can reach them.

tldr.problem: SIP servers normally open connections to User Agents to deliver requests, but firewalls, NATs and TLS server-certificate rules often make that impossible.
tldr.mechanism: The User Agent registers over connections it opens itself, tagging each with an instance-id and a reg-id, and keeps them alive with CRLF pings over TCP or STUN over UDP. Proxies send incoming requests back down those same flows.
tldr.outcome: A UA can register over several flows at once for reliability, and servers can route to it without connecting inward. RFC 5626 updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3327.

today: RFC 5626 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It itself updates RFC 3261 and RFC 3327.

sections.title: The Problem and the Key Idea
sections.content:
Many SIP deployments have User Agents (UAs) that can connect out to a registrar or proxy, but cannot be reached by connections in the reverse direction. The most likely cause is a NAT or firewall that only allows outgoing connections. Another is TLS: phones and PCs rarely have a stable DNS name suitable for a certificate, but they can still act as TLS clients and open outbound connections to a server that authenticates with its certificate.

The key idea is that when a UA sends a REGISTER or a dialog-forming request, the proxy can later reuse the same network flow (a UDP datagram pair, a TCP connection or similar) to forward incoming requests to that UA. Since the UA must then keep a flow alive, the RFC adds detection of flow failure, registration over multiple flows, and two keep-alive schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: The phone makes the call to the server first, and then the server answers back along the same line instead of trying to call the phone.

sections.title: Instance IDs, Reg-IDs and Flows
sections.content:
Each UA has a unique instance-id, a URN (the RFC says a UUID URN SHOULD be used) that MUST persist across power cycles and MUST NOT change when the device moves networks. It travels in the +sip.instance Contact parameter.

Each registration over a different flow also carries a reg-id Contact parameter, unique among that instance's registrations for the AOR. The sequence of reg-id values MUST be the same after every reboot so that new registrations collide with and replace the old ones. The registrar uses the instance-id to see that several bindings belong to one UA, and the reg-id to tell a new flow from a refreshed or replaced one.

A UA is configured with an outbound-proxy-set. It MUST support sets of at least two URIs and SHOULD support up to four, and MUST send REGISTER requests to at least two of them when the set has more than one. Each REGISTER uses a unique Call-ID and includes outbound and path option tags in Supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Your phone has a name tag that never changes, and a numbered ticket for each line it opens. If it reboots, it reuses the same tickets, so the server swaps old lines for new ones.

sections.title: Registering and Routing Over Flows
sections.content:
The UA examines successful registration responses for the outbound option tag in a Require header. If it is present, the registrar (and any edge proxy that needed to take part) supports the specification, and the UA starts keep-alives. If the first hop does not support outbound, a 439 (First Hop Lacks Outbound Support) response may come back, and the UA MAY retry without outbound or through another proxy.

An edge proxy that is the first hop MUST insert itself in a Path header with a flow token that is unique to the flow, or reject the request, and MUST add the ob URI parameter. The token can be any value that identifies the flow, recovers it and cannot be forged. The RFC gives a stateless example using a secret key and an HMAC-SHA1-80 over the flow's addresses and ports. If a token has been tampered with the proxy SHOULD answer 403; if the flow is gone it SHOULD answer 430 (Flow Failed).

The registrar binds an AOR to the combination of instance-id and reg-id, stores the Contact, its parameters and any Path values, and includes outbound in Require in its response. An authoritative proxy MUST NOT put more than one contact with the same AOR and instance-id in the target set at once. After a 430 it SHOULD try another contact with the same instance-id but a different reg-id.
sections.plainLanguage: The first helper outside the gate writes a secret note saying which line leads to the phone. Later, the note tells it which line to use, and nobody can fake the note.

sections.title: Keep-Alives and Flow Failure
sections.content:
Keep-alives refresh NAT and firewall bindings and let the UA detect that a flow has died. There are two kinds. Over connection-oriented transports such as TCP or SCTP the UA sends a double CRLF as a "ping" and the server replies with a single CRLF "pong". If no pong arrives within 10 seconds the flow is treated as failed. Over connectionless transports such as UDP the UA sends STUN Binding Requests on the same flow. The proxy or registrar acts as a limited STUN server on its SIP UDP port and its Binding Response MUST include XOR-MAPPED-ADDRESS. A STUN failure, or a change in that address, counts as flow failure.

If a successful registration response carries a Flow-Timer header, the UA MUST send keep-alives at least that often, and SHOULD randomize them between 80% and 100% of the value. Without it, the CRLF defaults are an upper bound of 120 seconds (lower bound 95) where battery is no concern and 840 seconds (lower bound 672) where it is. For STUN the default is a random 24 to 29 seconds.

A node MUST NOT send STUN to a next hop unless it has explicit indication that the hop supports this specification.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like saying "Still there?" down the phone every so often, and waiting for "Yes". If nobody says yes, the line is dead and you dial again.

sections.title: Flow Recovery and Backoff
sections.content:
When a flow fails, the UA forms a new one and each new registration MUST reuse the reg-id of the registration it replaces. To avoid the avalanche restart problem, where many UAs reconnect at once after a server fails, retries are delayed. The upper-bound wait is W = min(max-time, base-time * 2^consecutive-failures). The base-time defaults to 30 seconds if all flows to the outbound proxy set have failed and 90 seconds if at least one has not, and max-time defaults to 1800 seconds. The UA actually waits a uniform random time between 50 and 100% of W.

For example, with a base-time of 30 seconds and three failures, W is 240 seconds. When the UA boots it registers immediately, and if that fails and no other flow succeeds, the first retry comes 30 to 60 seconds later. Once the maximum is reached, the UA keeps trying indefinitely at random intervals of 15 to 30 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: If the line drops, you wait a bit before calling back, and wait longer after each failed try. Everyone waiting a different amount stops the server from being swamped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The key concern is that an attacker must not be able to hijack a valid user's sessions and receive that user's calls. The RFC aims to add no new attacks to existing SIP over UDP and TCP, not to prevent the attacks that already exist.

Without edge proxies, routing for an AOR changes only when a registration succeeds, so the scheme relies on SIP's existing registration authentication. Storing an instance-id without tying it to its AOR would not work, because an attacker could copy the instance-id. With edge proxies, the Path value is stored by the registrar only after successful authentication and returned later, and an edge proxy routes only over flows named in a flow token it created itself. The RFC changes no mandatory-to-implement security mechanisms: UAs already must implement Digest and should support TLS, and proxies must implement both.
sections.plainLanguage: The note only gets accepted if the person proves who they are first, so a stranger cannot trick the helpers into sending your calls to them.
